newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy govt to start crucial welfare talks on Tues.
newsitem.headline: Italy govt to start crucial welfare talks on Tues.

text.p: The centre-left government will start talks with unions on Tuesday over a reform of the welfare state which is seen as vital if Italy is to have any chance of becoming a founder member of the single European currency.

Labour Minister Tiziano Treu announced the starting date for the long-awaited negotiations at the weekend, as economic organisations, including the International Monetary Fund, renewed calls for an urgent overhaul of Italian social spending.

With the launch of European economic and monetary union union (EMU) drawing ever nearer, Prime Minister Romano Prodi still has much to do to tame the state deficit, which hit 6.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996.

Italy has pledged that this year it will reach the three percent goal laid down by the Maastricht Treaty for EMU hopefuls and has introduced some 78 trillion lire ($46.7 billion) of budget cuts in the last five months to meet that target.
But many of the measures are of a one-off nature and to ensure heavily-indebted Italy stays below the three percent threshold, so economists say social spending must be chopped.
"Our welfare sending has to be profoundly reviewed," Treu told reporters on Saturday. "It is clear that pension spending has most need to be reined in," he added.

The government is expected to indicate planned savings when it publishes its three-year economic programme for the period 1998-2000, later this month, and has said it wants to include social spending reforms in its 1998 budget.
But it faces huge opposition over the issue, especially on pensions, not just from the powerful unions but also from hardleft parliamentary ally, the Communist Refoundation.

The generous state pensions system was only reformed two years ago, and while most analysts argue that it is too slow moving, unions are determined to stick to an original clause saying the new set-up should not be reviewed until 1998.
Sergio D'Antoni, head of Italy's second largest union federation, the Cisl, was also quoted as saying on Sunday that Prodi must promise not to cut back social spending.
"If the government thinks it can be reduced, then the talks will finish before they've even begun," he said.

Communist Refoundation, which draws heavy support from Italy's army of pensioners, has also said it will brook no reduction in welfare spending, leaving many commentators sceptical about the chances of enacting meaningful reform.
But the pressure is on the Prodi government to move fast.

The European Commission forecast last month that Italy's 1998 deficit would be 3.9 percent of GDP, well outside the Maastricht ceiling, and La Repubblica newspaper reported on Sunday that the Commission was about to send Italy another tough warning to get its books in order or miss the EMU boat.
Newspapers also reported on Sunday that the IMF had sent a report to Prodi telling him to speed up pension reform.

Italy actually spends less than the European Union average on welfare spending, but many analysts believe the system is deeply unbalanced, with much of the cash earmarked for pensions at a time when the population is rapidly ageing.

On present trends, Italy's pensions bill is set to climb by 50 percent in 2010 before doubling again by 2030. Meanwhile, Italy's population between the ages of 15 and 70 is seen plunging to 36.68 million in 2030 from 42.86 million in 1995.
State pensions body INPs is running an annual deficit of around 80 trillion lire and unless things change, this is set to balloon given the population dynamics.
But to persuade unions and Refoundation to agree to a swift revision of the system will take all the government's persuasive skills. "It is going to be a long haul," Treu said. $1 = 1,671 lire
